items.claim: Subtracting the local timezone offset from every input breaks Python-supplied values (UTC-midnight ms timestamps) in all UTC- timezones: the picker now shows the previous day.
items.consequence: Python `DatePicker(value=date(2019, 9, 20))` serializes to 1568937600000 (2019-09-20T00:00Z). In a browser with TZ=America/Los_Angeles or America/New_York, the shifted time is 2019-09-19T17:00Z, so the picker displays 'Thu Sep 19 2019' while model.value is still Sep 20. Old code displayed Sep 20. Node run: old 'Fri Sep 20 2019', new 'Thu Sep 19 2019'. The same happens for a BokehJS ISO string '2019-09-20', and a null value (new Date(null), epoch 0) displays Dec 31 1969.

items.claim: min_date and max_date go through the same shifted conversion, so in UTC- timezones the selectable range moves one day earlier than the Python-specified bounds.
items.consequence: `DatePicker(min_date=date(2019, 9, 1), max_date=date(2019, 9, 30))` viewed in US Pacific: Pikaday gets minDate Aug 31 and maxDate Sep 29. The user can pick Aug 31, which is sent to the server although it is before min_date, and cannot pick Sep 30, which is a valid date.

items.claim: Timestamps with a time-of-day component are now converted to the browser-local calendar date instead of the date the user gave, so UTC+ browsers roll late-evening values forward a day.
items.consequence: `value=datetime(2019, 9, 20, 23, 30)` (the Date property accepts datetime) in Europe/Paris, Europe/London (BST) or Asia/Tokyo displays 'Sat Sep 21 2019'; old code displayed Sep 20. Likewise `max_date=datetime.utcnow()` (as used in the new tests) evaluated at 23:30Z lets a UTC+2 user pick tomorrow's date.

items.claim: The fix patches the symptom in `_unlocal_date` rather than the root cause: model.value has two incompatible representations (UTC ms from Python, local-time date string from `_on_select`) and one conversion cannot be right for both.
items.consequence: The old code was right for numeric UTC timestamps and wrong for the `toDateString()` string in UTC+; the new code is right for the string and wrong for numeric timestamps in UTC-. The durable fix is to branch on the value type in `_unlocal_date`, or have `_on_select` store a timezone-neutral value (e.g. `Date.UTC(y, m, d)` or 'YYYY-MM-DD' parsed by parts). Otherwise the off-by-one just moves to the other hemisphere.

items.claim: The new tests do not exercise the bug or the fix: they never vary the browser timezone and never assert the initially displayed value, so they pass with the pre-fix code on a UTC runner.
items.consequence: With TZ=UTC the old `_unlocal_date` yields 'Mon Sep 16 2019' for the click path, so `test_js_on_change_executes` passes without the change. No test checks that the input initially shows 'Fri Sep 20 2019', so the UTC- regression above is not caught even on a runner in a US timezone. Reverting the fix or regressing the initial display leaves CI green.

items.claim: The offset arithmetic plus ISO-string split/parse is now exactly equivalent to `new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth(), date.getDate())`, and the new comment wrongly calls the result timezone-agnostic.
items.consequence: Maintenance cost: seven lines of offset maths and string slicing hide that the function now truncates to local midnight, which is why UTC timestamps break. The 'agnostic to their local system's timezone' comment states the opposite of the behaviour and replaces the old comment that documented the 'date comes in as a UTC timestamp' invariant.

items.claim: `_unlocal_date` now mutates its argument in place with `date.setTime(...)` while also returning a new Date.
items.consequence: The three current callers pass throwaway `new Date(...)` objects, so nothing breaks today. Any future caller passing a Date it keeps (e.g. one held on the view, or the Date Pikaday hands to onSelect) would have it silently shifted by the timezone offset, and shifted again on each re-render. Using a local `const shifted = new Date(date.getTime() - offset)` avoids this.

items.claim: The tests build the widget from `datetime` values and a non-deterministic `datetime.utcnow()` for properties documented as date-only, and the file name departs from the sibling naming pattern.
items.consequence: `max_date=datetime.utcnow()` gives each run a different time-of-day bound, which under the new conversion maps to a different calendar day depending on browser timezone and time of run; `date(2019, 9, 30)` would be deterministic and match the 'Accept Date (but not DateTime)' contract. The file is `test_datepicker.py`, whereas siblings snake-case the class name (`test_color_picker.py`, `test_radio_button_group.py`), so `test_date_picker.py` would be the expected name.
